query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor reactive element addition of yttrium (~1 at.%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a Y-enriched interfacial layer at the oxide scale/substrate boundary, thereby enhancing scale adhesion and reducing oxygen ingress without compromising the alloy’s mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows good room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance but forms non‐protective, spallation‐prone oxide scales upon high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 1 atomic % Y (with a corresponding slight reduction in one of the refractory elements to preserve overall near-equiatomic balance).
generation.conditions: Samples are produced via conventional arc melting under inert atmosphere. Oxidation testing is conducted in static air at 800 °C (and optionally up to 1000 °C) for durations ranging from 5 to 100 hours, under low applied load or strain.
generation.structural_mediator: Yttrium, owing to its strong reactive element effect, is expected to segregate to the oxide/metal interface where it forms nanometric Y-rich oxides or alters the interfacial chemistry, reducing diffusivity and stress mismatch across the scale.
generation.mechanism: The reactive element effect is well known in high-temperature alloys: minor additions of elements like Y can modify the growth, morphology, and adhesion of oxide scales by segregating to grain boundaries and interfaces, thereby impeding rapid oxygen diffusion and scale spallation. In this refractory high-entropy system, Y is predicted to similarly enhance adherence and reduce oxidation rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Y-doped alloy should exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain (potentially a 20–40% decrease) and display a more continuous, adherent oxide scale with limited spallation, while retaining similar tensile ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy without Y addition, which develops mixed and less adherent oxide scales under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is restricted to a single compositional modification (addition of ~1 at.% Y) and is applicable for oxidation conditions at 800–1000 °C with exposure times up to 100 hours under low strain.
generation.uncertainty: The phase stability and segregation behavior of Y in the complex multi-principal element matrix are not fully characterized; unexpected interactions with the existing refractory elements could occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition and one with a modified composition including ~1 at.% Y (with minor compensatory changes). Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in static air at 800 °C for 5, 20, and 100 hours.
measurements: TGA to measure oxidation weight gain
Surface and cross-sectional analysis (SEM/EDS, TEM) to assess oxide scale morphology and verify Y segregation at the interface
Mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness measurements) to ensure bulk properties are maintained
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a significantly reduced oxidation weight gain or fails to develop a more adherent and continuous oxide scale, or if its mechanical performance degrades compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: For alloys like Inconel 625, solid-solution hardening is the main strengthening mechanism. Elements like Mo are important in this process. Nb and Ta can also contribute to solid solution strengthening to a lesser extent. In solid solution strengthening, Mo atoms are substituted into the γ matrix of Inconel alloys. Because Mo atoms have a significantly larger radius than those of Ni (209 pm and 163 pm, respectively), the substitution creates strain fields in the crystal lattice, which hinder the motion of dislocations, ultimately strengthening the material. The combination of elemental composition and strengthening mechanisms is why Inconel alloys can maintain their favorable mechanical and physical properties, such as high strength and fatigue resistance, at elevated temperatures, specifically those up to 650°C.

top3.builds_on: The well-established reactive element effect in high-temperature alloys (as used in alumina-forming superalloys) is here applied to a refractory high-entropy alloy system in a novel manner.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the specific incorporation of yttrium—an element not explored in the referenced Nb-silicide-based alloy studies—to tailor the oxide scale/substrate interface in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, thereby directly addressing the oxygen resistance limitation while preserving mechanical performance.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a minor reactive element addition of yttrium (~1 at.%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a Y-enriched interfacial layer at the oxide scale/substrate boundary, thereby enhancing scale adhesion and reducing oxygen ingress without compromising the alloy’s mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows good room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance but forms non‐protective, spallation‐prone oxide scales upon high-temperature exposure.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 1 atomic % Y (with a corresponding slight reduction in one of the refractory elements to preserve overall near-equiatomic balance).
fields.conditions: Samples are produced via conventional arc melting under inert atmosphere. Oxidation testing is conducted in static air at 800 °C (and optionally up to 1000 °C) for durations ranging from 5 to 100 hours, under low applied load or strain.
fields.structural_mediator: Yttrium, owing to its strong reactive element effect, is expected to segregate to the oxide/metal interface where it forms nanometric Y-rich oxides or alters the interfacial chemistry, reducing diffusivity and stress mismatch across the scale.
fields.mechanism: The reactive element effect is well known in high-temperature alloys: minor additions of elements like Y can modify the growth, morphology, and adhesion of oxide scales by segregating to grain boundaries and interfaces, thereby impeding rapid oxygen diffusion and scale spallation. In this refractory high-entropy system, Y is predicted to similarly enhance adherence and reduce oxidation rates.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Y-doped alloy should exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain (potentially a 20–40% decrease) and display a more continuous, adherent oxide scale with limited spallation, while retaining similar tensile ductility and yield strength.
fields.baseline: The standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy without Y addition, which develops mixed and less adherent oxide scales under the same conditions.
fields.boundary: The intervention is restricted to a single compositional modification (addition of ~1 at.% Y) and is applicable for oxidation conditions at 800–1000 °C with exposure times up to 100 hours under low strain.
fields.uncertainty: The phase stability and segregation behavior of Y in the complex multi-principal element matrix are not fully characterized; unexpected interactions with the existing refractory elements could occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition and one with a modified composition including ~1 at.% Y (with minor compensatory changes). Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in static air at 800 °C for 5, 20, and 100 hours.
measurements: TGA to measure oxidation weight gain
Surface and cross-sectional analysis (SEM/EDS, TEM) to assess oxide scale morphology and verify Y segregation at the interface
Mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness measurements) to ensure bulk properties are maintained
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a significantly reduced oxidation weight gain or fails to develop a more adherent and continuous oxide scale, or if its mechanical performance degrades compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: The known benefit of forming protective alumina scales via surface aluminizing, a method widely used in high-temperature superalloys and refractory alloys.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a surface engineering solution—pack aluminizing—as a single intervention to enhance the oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, leveraging the formation of an Al2O3 scale without altering the alloy’s bulk composition or properties, which has not been previously applied to this specific high-entropy system.

fields.hypothesis: A surface modification via pack aluminizing (aluminide coating) of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enhance its oxygen resistance by creating a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature oxidation.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which in its untreated state lacks sufficient oxygen resistance for high-temperature applications.
fields.intervention: Apply a pack cementation treatment with aluminum-containing media to form a diffusion-derived aluminide surface layer on the cast HfNbTaTiZr parts. This treatment is limited strictly to the near-surface region, leaving the bulk composition and mechanical performance largely unchanged.
fields.conditions: Oxidation tests conducted in air at 800–1200 °C for exposure durations ranging from 5 h to 100 h, under mechanical strains comparable to previously reported conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous aluminide layer that converts, upon oxidation, to a dense and slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale.
fields.mechanism: Alumina is one of the most stable and slow-growing oxides at high temperatures. The surface treatment induces an Al-rich sub-layer which, during initial oxidation, transforms into a protective Al2O3 scale that significantly impedes further oxygen ingress. Since the treatment is confined to the surface, the bulk mechanical properties remain essentially as those of the cast equiatomic alloy.
fields.predicted_outcome: The aluminized alloy is expected to show a marked reduction in oxidation weight gain, improved scale adherence, and a significant suppression of pesting phenomena at high temperatures, without compromising room- or high-temperature mechanical performance.
fields.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy which shows rapid oxygen ingress and poor scale integrity upon prolonged high-temperature exposure in air.
fields.boundary: Effective for high-temperature oxidation in air between 800 °C and 1200 °C and for exposure times up to 100 h. The process should not alter the near-bulk mechanical behavior.
fields.uncertainty: While aluminizing is well established in various alloys (e.g. for turbine blade coatings), its precise influence on a high-entropy refractory alloy such as HfNbTaTiZr in terms of interfacial reactions and potential residual stresses must be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples – one with pack aluminizing treatment and one untreated. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation in air at 1000 °C for 50–100 h. Characterize the oxide scale using SEM/EDS and measure the oxidation weight gains. Compare the mechanical properties (tensile tests) of both sets before and after exposure.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the alumina scale (SEM/EDS analysis)
Mechanical property retention (tensile and ductility tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pack aluminized samples do not show a significantly lower oxidation weight gain, exhibit poor scale adherence, or if their mechanical properties degrade substantially compared to untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s suggestion that further oxidation protection might be achievable via coatings (PMC7514121::web::020) and analogies from superalloy surface treatments as described in TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::003.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a surface-modification route—pack cementation aluminizing—specifically tailored for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, as opposed to bulk composition changes, to enhance oxidation resistance while preserving internal mechanical properties.

fields.hypothesis: A surface modification through pack cementation aluminizing treatment on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can improve its oxygen resistance by forming an enriched aluminide layer that readily forms a protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a homogeneous BCC single-phase microstructure and established room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
fields.intervention: Apply a pack cementation aluminizing treatment to the as-cast alloy, creating an Al-enriched surface layer without altering the bulk composition.
fields.conditions: Carry out the pack cementation process at a moderate temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for a specific duration to allow appropriate Al diffusion into the surface; then expose the treated samples to air at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: An Al-rich surface diffusion layer that transforms into a continuous alumina (Al2O3) scale upon further high-temperature exposure.
fields.mechanism: The pack process diffuses aluminum into the surface, forming an aluminide-rich zone. Upon subsequent high-temperature air exposure, this zone oxidizes preferentially to produce a dense and adherent alumina layer. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier, limiting oxygen ingress and thus preventing pesting while leaving the bulk BCC structure intact. This approach mirrors conventional practices in superalloy oxidation protection (e.g., TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::003).
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in oxidation resistance as demonstrated by reduced oxide scale growth and oxygen ingress after 5 h exposure at 800–1000 °C, while the underlying alloy retains its established mechanical performance.
fields.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (manifesting as pesting) under high-temperature air exposure.
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to be beneficial at temperatures in the 800–1000 °C range; excessively deep or uneven aluminizing could detrimentally affect near-surface microstructure and mechanical behavior.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters (temperature, time, and Al source concentration) for the pack treatment for this specific alloy are not fully established, which introduces some uncertainty regarding the uniformity and thickness of the aluminized layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and subject them to a pack cementation aluminizing treatment under controlled parameters. Compare these treated samples to untreated controls by exposing both to air at 900 °C for 5 hours. Characterize the surface oxide scales using microscopy and assess mechanical properties via compression or tensile tests.
measurements: Surface composition and layer thickness (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Mechanical properties post-treatment (ductility and yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples do not show a superior oxidation resistance (i.e., a more uniform and thinner protective alumina scale with less oxygen penetration) or if significant degradation in mechanical performance is observed relative to untreated samples, the hypothesis would be falsified.
